1.note: Zechariah is speaking to **Lebanon**, a place that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the coming destruction of the land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Lebanon. Alternate translation: [People of Lebanon, open your doors]

Zechariah is speaking of **fire** as if it were a living thing that could **devour** the trees. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that fire may burn up your cedars]

2.note: The word translated as **wail** copies the sound of crying or howling. Zechariah uses this word here, and a similar word about lions in verse 3, to make the scene sound sad and urgent, like people weeping and lions roaring. If your language has a word that sounds like crying, use it here. If not, choose words that still sound emotional and urgent, not calm or formal.

The word **cypress** refers to a tall evergreen tree, but its exact identification is uncertain; other translations render it as “fir,” “pine,” or “juniper.” If your readers would not be familiar with this kind of tree, you could use the name of a similar tall, valuable evergreen tree that they would recognize, or you could use a more general term, such as “large evergreen tree.” Alternate translation: [fir tree] or [pine tree]

Here Zechariah is speaking of the cypress trees as if they were a person who could **wail**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Cry out, cypress, like a mourner] or [Cypress, be greatly distressed]

2.q: הֵילֵ֤ל בְּרוֹשׁ֙ כִּֽי־נָ֣פַל אֶ֔רֶז אֲשֶׁ֥ר אַדִּרִ֖ים שֻׁדָּ֑דוּ הֵילִ֨ילוּ֙ אַלּוֹנֵ֣י בָשָׁ֔ן כִּ֥י יָרַ֖ד יַ֥עַר ה⁠בצור
2.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because the cedar has fallen, wail, cypress, since the majestic ones have been devastated! Because the fortified forest has gone down, wail, oaks of Bashan]

Zechariah is speaking of powerful rulers as if they were a **cedar** tree that had fallen. A cedar was one of the tallest, strongest trees in that area, so a fallen cedar pictures a powerful ruler who has lost his power. The text does not say exactly which ruler or nation this is, so keep your translation general instead of naming a specific person or place. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the powerful rulers have been overthrown]

The expression **have been devastated** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [enemies have devastated the majestic ones]

The word translated as **fortified** has a similar spelling to the word for **vintage/grape harvest**. Some ancient manuscripts and versions read this as “the forest of the vintage,” apparently confusing the two similar words. The ULT and UST follow the reading “the fortified forest” (i.e., an inaccessible or lofty forest), which matches the word form actually present here. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [the forest of the vintage has come down]

3.q: ק֚וֹל יִֽלְלַ֣ת הָ⁠רֹעִ֔ים כִּ֥י שֻׁדְּדָ֖ה אַדַּרְתָּ֑⁠ם ק֚וֹל שַׁאֲגַ֣ת כְּפִירִ֔ים כִּ֥י שֻׁדַּ֖ד גְּא֥וֹן הַ⁠יַּרְדֵּֽן
3.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. The word for glory here is a lot like the word for the “majestic ones” in verse 2. Zechariah repeats this idea to show that everything great and important, both the leaders and the land, has been completely ruined. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Listen to the shepherds wailing and the young lions roaring, for everything of value to them has been utterly devastated]

Zechariah is speaking of the rulers of the land as if they were **shepherds** and **young lions** that were wailing and roaring over what they had lost. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the crying of the rulers … the mourning of the powerful men]

Zechariah is using **the pride of the Jordan** as a common expression of the culture to mean the dense thickets of trees and bushes that grow along the Jordan River. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the dense thickets along the Jordan River are devastated]

4.note: Yahweh is speaking of leading and caring for the people as if that task were to **Shepherd** a flock of sheep. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Take care of]

Yahweh is speaking of the people of Israel as if they were a flock of sheep. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people who are marked for slaughter]

5.q: אֲשֶׁ֨ר קֹנֵי⁠הֶ֤ן יַֽהֲרְגֻ⁠ן֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א יֶאְשָׁ֔מוּ וּ⁠מֹכְרֵי⁠הֶ֣ן יֹאמַ֔ר
5.note: Here Yahweh is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The expression **are not held guilty** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and no one considers them guilty]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [say that Yahweh has blessed them, for they have become rich!]

6.note: Even though Yahweh is speaking, he refers to himself in the third person, using **the declaration of Yahweh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [the declaration that I, Yahweh, am making]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **declaration**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [this is what Yahweh declares]

6.q: אָנֹכִ֜י מַמְצִ֣יא אֶת־הָ⁠אָדָ֗ם אִ֤ישׁ בְּ⁠יַד־רֵעֵ֨⁠הוּ֙ וּ⁠בְ⁠יַ֣ד מַלְכּ֔⁠וֹ
6.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if he were causing people to **fall** into the power of their neighbors and king, as though pushing them down so that others could seize them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am handing mankind over, each man, to his neighbor and to his king]

Here the masculine terms **mankind** and **each man** have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [all people]

Here, **hand** represents power or control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [under the control of his neighbor and of his king … from their power]

7.note: Zechariah is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of sheep. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the suffering sheep of the flock]

7.q: לְ⁠אַחַ֞ד קָרָ֤אתִי נֹ֨עַם֙ וּ⁠לְ⁠אַחַד֙ קָרָ֣אתִי חֹֽבְלִ֔ים
7.note: The words **Favor** and **Union** are names that Zechariah gave to his two shepherd’s staffs. He chose names that carry meaning, since the staffs represent Yahweh’s relationship with the people.

8.note: The implication is that these **three shepherds** were leaders of the people whom Yahweh removed from their position. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the three leaders who were poorly shepherding the people]

Zechariah is using **my soul became short with them** as a common expression of the culture to mean that he became impatient with them. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I became tired of them]

9.note: Zechariah is repeating forms of the verbs **die** and **destroy** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that the flock is doomed and beyond saving. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Let the ones who are going to die, die, and let the ones who are going to be destroyed, be destroyed]

The expression **let it be destroyed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and let the one perishing perish]

Zechariah is speaking of the people as if they were sheep that would eat the flesh of one another. He means mean that they will turn against and destroy one another. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let each one destroy the other]

10.q: וָ⁠אֶקַּ֤ח אֶת־מַקְלִ⁠י֙ אֶת־נֹ֔עַם וָ⁠אֶגְדַּ֖ע אֹת֑⁠וֹ לְ⁠הָפֵיר֙ אֶת־בְּרִיתִ֔⁠י אֲשֶׁ֥ר כָּרַ֖תִּי אֶת־כָּל־הָ⁠עַמִּֽים
10.note: Here, **to** marks the words **break my covenant that I had cut with all the peoples** as the goal or purpose of his chopping up the **staff Favor**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

Zechariah is using the word **cut** as a common expression of the culture to mean “make,” since in that culture people spoke of making a covenant as cutting it. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my covenant that I had made]
This could mean: (1) all the nations of the world. Alternate translation: [all the world’s nations] (2) the Israelite nation. Alternate translation: [all of the Israelites]

11.note: The expression **it was broken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And I broke it]

The pronoun **it** refers to the covenant that Yahweh had made with all the peoples, mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the covenant was broken]

12.q: אִם־ט֧וֹב בְּ⁠עֵינֵי⁠כֶ֛ם הָב֥וּ שְׂכָרִ֖⁠י וְ⁠אִם־לֹ֣א ׀ חֲדָ֑לוּ
12.note: Zechariah is presenting a possible condition, that the people may or may not think it is good to give him his wages. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [If it is good in your eyes, then give my wages; but if it is not good, then refrain]

Zechariah is using **good in your eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean that something seems good or right to a person. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [If you consider it good]

In ancient times, a piece of silver was a coin or weight of silver called a shekel, which weighed about 11 grams, or about a third of an ounce. You could try to express this in terms of modern money values, but if you did, that could cause your Bible translation to become outdated and inaccurate, since those values can change over time. Instead, you might say something general like “thirty silver coins,” or give the equivalent weight, or use the term in the text and give the weight in a note.

13.note: A **potter** is a kind of craftsman who forms objects out of clay. If your readers would not be familiar with what a potter is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the craftsman who makes things out of clay … the craftsman who makes things out of clay]

Yahweh actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here, since thirty pieces of silver was in fact a contemptibly small price. It was also the amount the owner of an ox that gored a slave to death had to give to the owner of the slave (see Exo 21:32), so by paying that amount they were saying he was worth the same as a dead slave. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the contemptibly small price at which I was valued]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **price**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the magnificent silver]

14.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **brotherhood**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the brotherly ties]

15.note: Yahweh is speaking of a ruler of the people as if he were a shepherd. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the equipment of a foolish ruler]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **foolish shepherd**. He means foolish shepherds in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [foolish shepherds]

16.note: Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [illustrating that]

16.q: הַ⁠נִּכְחָד֤וֹת לֹֽא־יִפְקֹד֙ הַ⁠נַּ֣עַר לֹֽא־יְבַקֵּ֔שׁ וְ⁠הַ⁠נִּשְׁבֶּ֖רֶת לֹ֣א יְרַפֵּ֑א הַ⁠נִּצָּבָה֙ לֹ֣א יְכַלְכֵּ֔ל וּ⁠בְשַׂ֤ר הַ⁠בְּרִיאָה֙ יֹאכַ֔ל וּ⁠פַרְסֵי⁠הֶ֖ן יְפָרֵֽק
16.note: Zechariah uses a repetitive series of clauses here to communicate that what he is saying should be understood as comprehensive and overwhelming. Use a form in your language that someone would use to describe a situation that is comprehensive and overwhelming.

Here Zechariah is speaking as if the strongest, healthiest members of the people were **the fat one**, a well-fed sheep. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the best-fed sheep] or [the strongest of the people]

Yahweh is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look, I am raising up a shepherd in the land]

17.note: Yahweh is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of distress and warning of coming judgment. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Alas]

Here, **his arm** represents the shepherd’s strength and **his right eye** represents his ability to see. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [against his strong arm and against his seeing right eye]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [May a sword strike his arm and his right eye]
Here, **A sword** represents “a violent attack.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [A violent attack]

17.q: זְרֹע⁠וֹ֙ יָב֣וֹשׁ תִּיבָ֔שׁ וְ⁠עֵ֥ין יְמִינ֖⁠וֹ כָּהֹ֥ה תִכְהֶֽה
17.note: Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [his arm will surely wither, and his right eye will surely grow dim]
